storm.summary_layperson: No storms on radar this evening — skies are clear and any thunderstorm activity is focused well to the west of the New York City area, leaving the cove in a quiet window through 10 PM.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Long Island Sound water (73°F) is only 7°F cooler than inland air (81°F) — a weak stabilizing influence, but not strong enough to actively deflect storms, and none are approaching today.
storm.detail_html:
Radar is clear as of 4:14 PM EDT — no storm cells anywhere in the KOKX coverage area and no incoming precipitation. CAPE (atmospheric energy available for thunderstorms) is very low at 30 J/kg this afternoon, well below the 1,500 J/kg threshold that typically produces organized convection.

The NWS forecast discussion (OKX, 3:07 PM EDT) flags a slow-moving low pressure system that will bring unsettled weather with showers and embedded thunderstorms from Monday night into Thursday. For this afternoon and evening, activity is described as mainly confined to north and west of the NYC terminals — Riverside and Greenwich sit to the northeast and should largely miss the afternoon pulse. The low's influence will be felt more strongly overnight and into Tuesday.

CAPE does increase through the window per model guidance, reaching roughly 340–380 J/kg by 8–9 PM EDT. That is still modest — well below the 1,500 J/kg convective threshold — and with bulk wind shear at only 15.6 kt (below the 20 kt threshold for organized storm development), any isolated cells that develop should be short-lived pulse-type with brief life cycles.

Long Island Sound water is 73°F versus 81°F inland — a 7°F air–water gap. This creates a weak stabilizing marine layer over the Sound. However, the protective mechanism is not meaningfully active today: the gap falls below the roughly 10°F level where the Sound reliably deflects or chokes incoming convection. With no cells approaching, this is largely academic for the 5–10 PM window. If a cell develops to the southwest after 8 PM as instability builds, the weak marine layer offers only partial protection — less than on a classic summer afternoon when the water–air gap is larger.

wind.tactics_blurb: A 4–5 kt ESE-to-E drifter window for the first part of the evening, with the cove progressively sheltered by Greenwich Point as the direction backs toward ENE by sunset. Stay central — a sharp shift to S is expected around 9 PM on a trough passage, and anyone committed deep on the east side will find themselves badly placed for the new wind.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a light gradient wind evening. The sea-breeze ingredients are marginally present — the air–water temperature difference (deltaT) of 7.2°F is just above the 5°F gate that enables a thermal sea breeze — but the sea breeze hasn't established convincingly: only 29% of coastal stations are blowing southerly, and the HRRR model forecast shows the wind backing counterclockwise (SE→E→ENE) through the evening rather than veering clockwise toward S–SSW as a mature sea breeze would. This is gradient wind responding to a slow-moving low approaching from the west, not a thermal. Because this is a gradient-wind day rather than a sea-breeze day, the sea-breeze direction correction that adjusts for HRRR's known directional bias does not apply here — raw HRRR directions are used throughout.

For the first half of the window (5–8 PM EDT), expect light ESE-to-E at 4–5 kt. As the direction backs from ESE toward E and then ENE, the cove falls increasingly into Greenwich Point's (Tod's Point's) shelter. On due-E flow, the entire cove sits behind the Greenwich Point peninsula — open Long Island Sound may appear breezy while the start area is relatively calm. APRS stations upwind to the east confirm this: GW4252 (3 miles east) is reading essentially calm with 4-kt gusts; DW1086 (15 miles ESE) shows only 1.7 kt mean. The surface-layer wind is shallow. RYC's current 4.6 kt (10-min avg 4.9 kt) is the best estimate of what the fleet will actually sail in.

The key event of the window is a sharp direction swing around 9 PM EDT. HRRR shows the wind jumping from roughly 77° ENE to 189° S in a single hour — a 112° clockwise shift. This is the signature of a surface trough passage, consistent with the NWS forecast discussion noting a weak surface trough developing in the vicinity Monday afternoon and evening. Once the trough passes, the gradient flow settles to a southerly direction at 5–6 kt. S flow is the cleanest for the cove's north–south axis: no Greenwich Point shelter effect, steadier pressure throughout the course. The post-trough S wind is the best sailing of the evening, though still on the light side.

Tactical approach: stay central for the early part of the program. The direction is backing through a range where different sides of the course get progressively less wind (E flow puts the whole cove in shadow), making positional advantages minimal and directional shifts the dominant factor. Boats that pin the east side early sit in the deepest shadow of Greenwich Point on E/ENE flow and need a long tack back when the S fills in. Boats on the west side gain leverage on the backing shift but risk being on the wrong side of the trough passage. Center keeps both options open. After the trough, commit to the lifted tack on the post-trough S wind and treat it as a steadier, more uniform gradient. The trough timing carries roughly ±1-hour uncertainty on a weak synoptic feature — watch RYC live starting around 8:30 PM for the ENE-to-S shift as the leading edge arrives.

Wind-for-racing assessment: the 4–5 kt window (5–9 PM) is squarely drifter-class — manageable but finicky, light-air specialist territory. The post-trough 5–6 kt S wind after 9 PM is marginally better and steadier. RC should plan conservatively for the early races and watch for the trough-induced improvement before committing to late races.
